rule: The header is exactly: Account, Month, Statement received, Printed opening, Printed closing, Imported, Reconciled, Books closing, Notes
why it matters: The checker reads columns by name. A renamed or missing column means a whole kind of check silently stops.

rule: Month is YYYY-MM and each account has one row per month
why it matters: Months sort as text. Jul 2026 sorts before Jun 2026, which puts the chain out of order.

rule: Statement received, Imported and Reconciled are Yes, No or blank
why it matters: A Y or a tick mark reads as No, so a done month shows as still to do.

rule: A received statement has its printed opening and closing balance. The first row per account (the month you trust) needs its closing
why it matters: Those two balances are the proof. Without them the chain can't be checked.

rule: Balances are plain numbers: no dollar sign, no thousands comma
why it matters: Formatted numbers can't be compared to the cent.

rule: A month marked Reconciled is also Imported and its books closing equals the printed closing
why it matters: Reconciled means it ties. A month marked done that doesn't tie hides the one problem the tracker exists to find.

rule: Each statement opens at the previous statement's closing balance
why it matters: When months are missing the jump is their combined net change, which tells you what to look for. With nothing missing it is a wrong or mistyped statement.

rule: Every month from the month you trust through the catch-up month has its statement
why it matters: Missing statements are the usual reason a catch-up stalls. Older ones can take a week or two to arrive, so ask on day one.
A difference carried into the next month gets harder to find with every month added on top.

rule: The month you trust ties: its books closing equals its printed closing
why it matters: If the starting point doesn't tie the job is a cleanup first, not a catch-up.
A month reconciled while an earlier one is open has to be checked again when the earlier month changes.
